title: Myelodysplastic Syndromes
subject: Pathology
summary: MDS are clonal marrow disorders causing ineffective hematopoiesis and cytopenias. Diagnosis relies on dysplasia, cytogenetics and blast count. Management balances transfusion support, disease‑modifying agents and stem‑cell transplant.

sections.p: MDS are clonal disorders of multipotent hematopoietic stem cells that produce dysplastic, ineffective blood cells. The WHO 2022 criteria require dysplasia in ≥10 % of one or more lineages, no blast‑count ≥20 % and exclusion of other causes.

t.b: Key for diagnosis and risk stratification

sections.p: Risk is stratified by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS‑R). It uses cytopenia severity, blast percentage and cytogenetics to predict survival and AML progression.
b: High – >10 % blasts or very adverse cytogenetics

sections.p: Idiopathic in most cases. Secondary causes include prior alkylating chemotherapy, ionising radiation, chronic hepatitis B, HIV, schistosomiasis, and herbal toxins common in low‑resource settings.
Patients often present with fatigue, pallor, recurrent infections, easy bruising or bleeding. Anemia is usually normocytic or macrocytic with normal iron studies.
Key tests are CBC, peripheral smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy with cytogenetics, and flow cytometry. In low‑resource settings, a peripheral smear and basic karyotype may suffice.
Rapid cytopenia worsening, unexplained fever, bleeding, or splenomegaly suggest progression to AML or severe marrow failure.
Treat underlying cause, provide transfusion support, consider disease‑modifying agents (e.g., azacitidine, decitabine) and evaluate for stem‑cell transplant. Avoid drugs that worsen cytopenias.
b: Treat underlying cause (e.g., antiviral therapy for HBV)
Consider allogeneic stem‑cell transplant in eligible patients

t.b: Similar to azacitidine, used when azacitidine unavailable

sections.p: Regular CBCs every 3–6 months, monitor cytogenetics if changing, and counsel on avoiding further marrow toxins. Early detection of progression allows timely transplant.
Aplastic anemia, severe infection with leukemoid reaction, and iron‑deficiency anemia can mimic MDS.
b: Aplastic anemia – hypocellular marrow, no dysplasia
Leukemoid reaction – reactive neutrophilia, no dysplasia

sections.p: Macrocytosis may be mistaken for B12/folate deficiency; iron studies can be normal despite anemia; cytogenetics may be normal in 30 % of cases.
b: Normal iron studies – rule out deficiency

t.b: Normal in MDS, low in iron deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Bleeding or bruising that does not resolve
Rapid weight loss or night sweats

faq.a: Allogeneic stem‑cell transplant is the only curative option, but it is reserved for fit patients with high‑risk disease.
They reverse DNA methylation, restoring normal gene expression and reducing blasts.
MDS can still exist; rely on morphology, blast count and clinical picture.

exam: A 68‑year‑old man with chronic anemia and neutropenia has a peripheral smear showing macrocytosis and hypogranular neutrophils. What is the next best step? — Bone marrow aspirate with cytogenetics to confirm MDS and risk stratify.

A patient with known MDS presents with sudden drop in platelets and mucosal bleeding. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — AML transformation; urgent transfusion and consider hypomethylating therapy.

Why is B12 deficiency ruled out in a patient with macrocytosis and normal ferritin? — Macrocytosis in MDS is due to ineffective erythropoiesis, not vitamin deficiency; B12 levels should be checked but are often normal.

A patient with prior alkylating chemotherapy develops pancytopenia. How do you differentiate aplastic anemia from MDS? — Bone marrow cellularity (hypocellular in aplastic anemia, hypercellular with dysplasia in MDS).
Which cytogenetic abnormality is associated with the best prognosis in MDS? — Deletion 5q; patients may respond well to lenalidomide.
A low‑resource hospital has no flow cytometry. How would you diagnose MDS? — Use CBC, peripheral smear, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy and karyotype; morphology and blast count suffice for diagnosis.
